extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers of English literature; readers/scholars of Addison & Steele
extracted.subtask_description: An editorial/introduction to The Spectator (Addison & Steele) describing the authors, historical context, and qualities of their writing; aimed at explaining what makes their work significant and how it exemplifies good literary practice. Extracts implicit evaluative standards for prose and criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sympathy with the people
rubrics_metrics.description: “his sympathies were with all England.” (Steele’s sympathies were with all England; he saw literature as speaking for the people and looking to the people for approval and support.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writing should address and sympathize with ordinary readers and social realities; favour subjects and tone that engage public concerns rather than only elite patronage. Anti-pattern: writing that is remote from the populace or only for elite patrons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious earnestness / moral seriousness
rubrics_metrics.description: The introduction repeatedly links the value of the work to a shared ‘religious earnestness’, stating this moral seriousness is among “the foundations of this book, its Monument.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prose that is grounded in sincere moral or religious conviction lends weight and unity to essays; moral seriousness can be an asset when balanced with wit. Anti-pattern: vacuous piety or insincere moralizing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sportive, delicately whimsical humour
rubrics_metrics.description: Addison’s style is praised as being “enlivened with the free play of that sportive humour, delicately whimsical and gaily wise.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use light, playful humour to enliven serious criticism; humour should be gracefully integrated (delicate/whimsical) rather than coarse. Scoring note: humour that aids clarity and engagement is a positive; humour that obscures argument or offends is negative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural thought and speech / plain-strength (Saxon roots)
rubrics_metrics.description: The text praises a movement toward “natural thought and speech” and suggests critics should ‘look back to the chief source of their language ... not Latin but Saxon’ to give strength and harmony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor plain, strong, native diction and natural expression over artificial Latinate/Frenchified phrasing; clarity and vernacular force are marks of good prose. Anti-pattern: overly pedantic, foreign-influenced diction that weakens rhetorical power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid didactic manner / do not be over-moralizing
rubrics_metrics.description: Steele’s earlier work is described as “too didactic. It was indeed plain truth... but an air of superiority, freely allowed only to the professional man teaching rules of his own art, belongs to a too didactic manner.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not adopt a preachy or superior tone; show principles through example and lively writing rather than lecturing. Anti-pattern: heavy-handed instruction that alienates readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive dependence on classical quotation
rubrics_metrics.description: Of Addison’s travel notes: he ‘crammed his pages with quotation from Virgil and Horace… an overdose of its own physic for all ills of literature.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use classical references judiciously; allow original observation and voice to dominate. Anti-pattern: overloading prose with citations or learned allusion at the expense of fresh content and reader engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance refinement with popular appeal (audience awareness)
rubrics_metrics.description: The book contrasts two career paths: the polished patronage route (Addison) and the rough, popular track (Steele), noting Steele’s success by serving the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be clear about intended audience and strike an appropriate balance between cultivated refinement and accessibility to wider readers. Scoring note: success may be measured by how well style and content fit intended readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical impartiality / beware sympathy blinding judgement
rubrics_metrics.description: The introduction warns that ‘the same strong sympathy with Blackmore's purpose in it blinded Dr. Johnson also to the failure of this poem,’ noting sympathy can mislead criticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain critical distance; sympathetic motives should not prevent honest appraisal of merits and flaws. Anti-pattern: allowing personal or ideological sympathy to excuse poor work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analytic depth / relish for analysis of thought
rubrics_metrics.description: Addison is described as one who ‘relishes analysis of thought,’ inclined to speculation and careful analysis rather than merely ornament.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good critical prose should include thoughtful analysis and intellectual rigor—explain reasoning and dissect subjects clearly. Scoring note: depth of analysis is valued, provided it remains accessible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincere wit without cant
rubrics_metrics.description: Steele ‘gave unostentatiously a lively wit to the true service of religion, without having spoken or written ... a word of mere religious cant.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for genuine, understated wit that supports subject matter; avoid insincere or hackneyed piety (cant). Anti-pattern: rhetorical flourishes that mask shallow sentiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write to amend contemporary tastes / cultural usefulness
rubrics_metrics.description: Addison’s genius is said to be ‘serviceable in amendment of the tastes of his own time,’ implying literature should help improve public taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work that refines or elevates public taste—while remaining understandable—earns credit; literature can have educative/corrective aims. Scoring note: influence on readers’ tastes and manners is a positive indicator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resist blind adherence to fashionable foreign critical rules
rubrics_metrics.description: The introduction criticizes earlier English writers for being ‘submissive to the new strength of the critical genius of France’ and urges returning to native linguistic sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid uncritical imitation of foreign fashions; evaluate and adopt methods that suit one’s language and audience. Anti-pattern: slavish following of outside critical orthodoxies that conflict with local literary strengths.
